implementation_notes: The .NET default is a persistence-ignorant POCO model plus EF Core configuration kept outside the classes: one IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> per aggregate in a Persistence/Configurations folder, registered with ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly, maps table and column names, value conversions and value objects (OwnsOne/OwnsMany) without putting a single attribute on the domain type. EF Core materialises encapsulated aggregates through private constructors and backing fields (PropertyAccessMode.Field), so the model keeps its invariants while the ORM still does the mapping - the mapper is replaced by configuration classes, and the classic hand-written mapper is only needed when the storage shape and the model genuinely diverge.
pitfalls: EF Core still shapes the model: navigation properties, a private parameterless constructor and backing-field access are concessions to the mapper, and lazy-loading proxies require virtual members throughout the aggregate.
A repository that returns IQueryable<T> or tracked entities hands the persistence layer back to callers and defeats the separation even though no attribute was used.

Owned types have restrictions (no DbSet, no sharing one instance between owners, no inheritance), so some DDD value-object shapes cannot be mapped as owned types and force a separate persistence model.

variants.name: Explicit persistence model with Dapper and hand-written mappers
variants.idiom_name: DAO / persistence model classes + repository mapping with Dapper
variants.implementation_notes: Where the schema is legacy, messy or must be versioned per row (document stores), the honest form is an explicit persistence model: DAO classes that correspond 1:1 with tables or document versions, mapped by the ORM or by Dapper, plus hand-written mapping between DAOs and the domain model inside repositories. This keeps the domain clean even when no ORM could map it directly, at the price of reimplementing part of what an ORM already does - which is precisely the trade-off that makes this the exceptional variant rather than the default in .NET.
pitfalls: A full DAO layer re-creates the ORM: every field is mapped twice, and joins, identity and change tracking must be written by hand.
SQL strings in repositories drift from the DAO definitions - round-trip tests are the only guard against silent column mismatches.
